questions.question: What did nurses want from the citations in the prior auth drafts?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion in the draft. [1] They viewed these citations as essential for understanding the basis of each claim in the draft. [2] Nurses used the citations to verify that the draft accurately reflected the information in the patient's chart. [2] They would open each citation and read the corresponding chart entry to ensure it supported the claim made in the draft. [2]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt: [MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.

questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

seeded.answer:
Clinicians' biggest pain point with documentation is the burden it places on their time. [1] Documentation burden was ranked as the #1 contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%). [1] 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day. [1]

Clinicians also expressed concerns about the accuracy and completeness of AI-drafted notes. [2] Scribe-drafted notes often capture what was discussed in the visit but leave out the specificity coding depends on: laterality, acute vs. chronic, type or stage (they gave heart failure type and CKD stage as examples), and the "due to" link between two conditions. [2] When it's missing the coder has two options, query the physician or code to the unspecified level, and they said they are doing both more often than with notes physicians typed from their own templates. [2] They noted the July 2025 prototype's mismatches were mostly at the specificity level too, and expect a suggester reading these notes to hit the same wall. [2]

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt: Earlier ambient-scribe research looked at what the scribe gets wrong: medication dosages and sound-alike drug names, and whether clinicians trust the draft enough to skim it. Two sessions touched on what the scribe takes in more broadly. In an October 2025 contextual inquiry, a behavioral health clinician said that any AI tool listening to or drafting behavioral health session notes raises consent and 42 CFR Part 2 questions (2025-10-07-contextual-inquiry-behavioral-health-sensitive-notes/session-notes.md:28); the exclusion of that population from the near-term ambient scribe rollout is recorded in the scope-boundaries finding (scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md:72-74). A care coordinator said the visit notes they read since GA are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31). Neither asked the person signing a draft about content the scribe writes down correctly but that doesn't belong in a visit note: small talk, a patient's remarks about other people, side conversations with a family member in the room. This session asked a primary care physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, what of that kind ends up in their drafts and what they remove before they sign.

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Share with the ambient scribe team that the confidence underline doesn't help with incidental content, because that content is usually transcribed accurately; reviewing for it means reading the whole draft.
If anything is designed for this, explore pointing out lines that may not belong in the note rather than removing them, so the clinician makes the call.
Keep this separate from the transcription-confidence work: it is about what belongs in the note, not whether it was heard correctly.
